question: What is the maximum number of open CAPAs a device manufacturer may have under the QMSR?
ideal_answer:
The QMSR sets no maximum number of open CAPAs. There is no numeric limit on open corrective and preventive actions anywhere in 21 CFR Part 820; the only paragraph in the part that uses that vocabulary at all is in 820.3, Definitions.

Part 820 as amended consists of six live sections - 820.1 Scope, 820.3 Definitions, 820.7 Incorporation by reference, 820.10 Requirements for a quality management system, 820.35 Control of records, and 820.45 Device labeling and packaging controls - and none of them imposes a count-based limit. Corrective and preventive action reaches the manufacturer through ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7, which likewise sets requirements for the process rather than a ceiling on the number of open actions.

A large or growing number of open CAPAs may be a finding about the effectiveness of the system, but it is not a breach of a numeric limit, because no such limit exists.

(a)(1) (1) Timely and effective identification, communication, and evaluation of events that may be subject to MDR requirements;
(a)(2) (2) A standardized review process or procedure for determining when an event meets the criteria for reporting under this part; and
(a)(3) (3) Timely transmission of complete medical device reports to manufacturers or to us, or to both if required.
(b) (b) Documentation and recordkeeping requirements for:
(b)(1) (1) Information that was evaluated to determine if an event was reportable;
(b)(2) (2) All medical device reports and information submitted to manufacturers and/or us;
(b)(4) (4) Systems that ensure access to information that facilitates timely followup and inspection by us.

[21 CFR 803.18] What are the requirements for establishing and maintaining MDR files or records that apply to me?
(a) (a) If you are a user facility, importer, or manufacturer, you must establish and maintain MDR event files. You must clearly identify all MDR event files and maintain them to facilitate timely access.
(b)(1) (b)(1) For purposes of this part, “MDR event files” are written or electronic files maintained by user facilities, importers, and manufacturers. MDR event files may incorporate references to other information (e.g., medical records, patient files, engineering reports), in lieu of copying and maintaining duplicates in this file. Your MDR event files must contain:
(c) (c) If you are a user facility, you must retain an MDR event file relating to an adverse event for a period of 2 years from the date of the event. If you are a manufacturer or importer, you must retain an MDR event file relating to an adverse event for a period of 2 years from the date of the event or a period of time equivalent to the expected life of the device, whichever is greater. If the device is no longer distributed, you still must maintain MDR event files for the time periods described in this paragraph (c).
(d)(2) (2) You must retain copies of the required device incident records for a period of 2 years from the date of inclusion of the record in the file or for a period of time equivalent to the expected life of the device, whichever is greater. You must maintain copies of these records for this period even if you no longer distribute the device.
(e) (e) If you are a manufacturer, you may maintain MDR event files as part of your complaint file, under part 820 of this chapter, if you prominently identify these records as MDR reportable events. We will not consider your submitted MDR report to comply with this part unless you evaluate an event in accordance with the quality management system requirements described in part 820 of this chapter. You must document and maintain in your MDR event files an explanation of why you did not submit or could not obtain any information required by this part, as well as the results of your evaluation of each event.

Written procedures (21 CFR 803.17). A user facility, importer or manufacturer must develop, maintain and implement written MDR procedures covering internal systems providing for timely and effective identification, communication and evaluation of events that may be subject to MDR requirements; a standardized review process for determining when an event meets the reporting criteria; and timely transmission of complete medical device reports to manufacturers or to FDA (803.17(a)). They must also cover documentation and recordkeeping for the information evaluated to determine reportability, the reports and information submitted, information evaluated in preparing annual reports, and systems ensuring access to information for timely follow-up and inspection (803.17(b)).

MDR event files (803.18). These must be established, clearly identified and maintained to facilitate timely access (803.18(a)). They must hold information or references relating to the adverse event, including all documentation of the deliberations and decision-making used to decide whether a device-related death, serious injury or malfunction was reportable; copies of all reports submitted; and copies of FDA's electronic acknowledgments (803.18(b)(1)).

Retention (803.18(c)). A user facility must retain an MDR event file for 2 years from the date of the event. A manufacturer or importer must retain it for 2 years from the date of the event or for a period equivalent to the expected life of the device, whichever is greater.

question: Under what conditions may an investigation proceed with an exception from informed consent for emergency research?
ideal_answer:
21 CFR 50.24 permits it only on a defined set of IRB findings. The IRB responsible for review, approval and continuing review may approve the investigation without requiring informed consent from all subjects only if it finds, with the concurrence of a licensed physician who is a member of or consultant to the IRB and is not otherwise participating, all of the following (50.24(a)).

The conditions. Obtaining informed consent is not feasible because the subjects will not be able to give it as a result of their medical condition, and the intervention under investigation must be administered before consent from their legally authorized representatives is feasible (50.24(a)(2)(i), (ii)). Participation holds out the prospect of direct benefit to the subjects because they are facing a life-threatening situation that necessitates intervention (50.24(a)(3)(i)). And the investigation could not practicably be carried out without the waiver (50.24(a)(4)).

Community consultation and public disclosure (50.24(a)(7)). Additional protections are required, including public disclosure to the communities in which the investigation will be conducted and from which subjects will be drawn, before initiation, of the plans for the investigation and its risks and expected benefits (50.24(a)(7)(ii)); and public disclosure of sufficient information after completion to apprise the community and researchers of the study, including the demographic characteristics of the research population, and its results (50.24(a)(7)(iii)).

Two procedural requirements. Protocols involving this exception must be performed under a separate IND or IDE that clearly identifies them as protocols that may include subjects who are unable to consent (50.24(d)). And if an IRB determines it cannot approve the investigation because it does not meet the 50.24(a) criteria or because of other relevant ethical concerns, it must document its findings and provide them promptly as the paragraph directs (50.24(e)).

question: What is the difference between a Substantial Equivalence report, an Exemption from SE request, and a PMTA?
ideal_answer:
Three different routes to market, and the evidence here speaks directly to the middle one.

Substantial equivalence report. The first route is a report under section 905(j)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, intended to demonstrate that a new tobacco product is substantially equivalent within the meaning of section 910 - that is, a comparison against a predicate tobacco product that can be legally marketed.

Exemption from SE (21 CFR 1107.1). Under section 905(j)(3) of the Act, FDA may exempt a tobacco product from the requirements relating to demonstrating substantial equivalence where the modification would be a minor modification of a legally marketed tobacco product (1107.1(a)(1)); a report under section 905(j)(1) is not necessary to ensure that permitting the product to be marketed would be appropriate for protection of the public health (1107.1(a)(2)); and an exemption is otherwise appropriate (1107.1(a)(3)). A request may be made only by the manufacturer of a legally marketed tobacco product, and only for a minor modification to that product (1107.1(b)). It must identify the products, explain in detail why the modification is minor and why an SE report is unnecessary, and include a certification signed by a responsible official summarising the supporting evidence and the rationale for the determination that the modification does not increase the product's appeal to or use by minors, its toxicity or its addictiveness (1107.1(b)(2), (5), (6), (7)).

PMTA. The third route is a premarket tobacco product application, which does not rest on a predicate at all: it stands on its own evidence that marketing the product would be appropriate for the protection of the public health.

So the distinction is: SE compares to a predicate; an SE exemption dispenses with that comparison for a minor modification on the three 1107.1(a) conditions; a PMTA proceeds independently of any predicate.

question: What meaning does Part 820 give to the term 'safety and performance' as it is used in the incorporated standard?
evidence:
[21 CFR 820.3] Definitions.
— The definitions in ISO 13485 and in Clause 3 of ISO 9000 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) apply to this part, except as specified in paragraph (b) of this section, and do not affect the meaning of similar terms defined in this title.
(a) (a) The following terms, which are either not used or not defined in ISO 13485 or in Clause 3 of ISO 9000, also apply for the purposes of this part:
(a) Batch or lot means one or more components or finished devices that consist of a single type, model, class, size, composition, or software version that are manufactured under essentially the same conditions and that are intended to have uniform characteristics and quality within specified limits.
(a) Component means any raw material, substance, piece, part, software, firmware, labeling, or assembly that is intended to be included as part of the finished, packaged, and labeled device.
(a) Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act means the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, 21 U.S.C. 321 et seq., as amended.
(a) Finished device means any device or accessory to any device that is suitable for use or capable of functioning, whether or not it is packaged, labeled, or sterilized.
(a) Human cell, tissue, or cellular or tissue-based product (HCT/P) regulated as a device means an HCT/P as defined in § 1271.3(d) of this chapter that does not meet the criteria in § 1271.10(a) of this chapter and that is also regulated as a device.
(a) Remanufacturer means any person who processes, conditions, renovates, repackages, restores, or does any other act to a finished device that significantly changes the finished device's performance or safety specifications, or intended use.
(b) (b) All definitions in section 201 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act shall apply to the regulation of quality management systems under this part and shall supersede the correlating terms and definitions in ISO 13485 (e.g., the definitions of device and labeling in section 201(h) and (m) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act apply to this part and supersede the definitions for the correlating terms in ISO 13485 (labelling and medical device)). In addition, the following terms and definitions apply to this part and supersede the definitions for the correlating terms in ISO 13485 or ISO 9000:
(b) Implantable medical device shall have the meaning of “implant” as defined in section 860.3 of this chapter.
(b) Organization shall have the meaning of “manufacturer” as defined in this part.
(b) Safety and Performance shall have the meaning of “safety and effectiveness” in Clause 0.1 of ISO 13485. The phrase “safety and performance” does not relieve a manufacturer from any obligation to implement controls or other measures that provide reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness.
ideal_answer:
21 CFR 820.3(b) supplies the meaning. "Safety and Performance" shall have the meaning of "safety and effectiveness" in Clause 0.1 of ISO 13485, and the phrase "safety and performance" does not relieve a manufacturer from any obligation to implement controls or other measures that provide reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness.

So the term is not a softer standard. FDA has mapped the standard's vocabulary onto its own: where the incorporated standard says "safety and performance", read "safety and effectiveness", which is the statutory and regulatory test.

This sits in a general rule about vocabulary. The definitions in ISO 13485 and in Clause 3 of ISO 9000 apply to the part, except as specified in 820.3(b), and do not affect the meaning of similar terms defined elsewhere in this title (820.3). And all definitions in section 201 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act apply to the regulation of quality management systems under the part and supersede the correlating terms and definitions in ISO 13485 - for example the definitions of device and labeling in section 201(h) and (m) (820.3(b)).

Two other mappings in the same paragraph work the same way: "Organization" has the meaning of "manufacturer" as defined in the part, and "Implantable medical device" has the meaning of "implant" as defined in 860.3.

(b) (b) You must conduct a reanalysis of the food safety plan as a whole, or the applicable portion of the food safety plan:
(b)(1) (1) Whenever a significant change in the activities conducted at your facility creates a reasonable potential for a new hazard or creates a significant increase in a previously identified hazard;
(b)(2) (2) Whenever you become aware of new information about potential hazards associated with the food;
(b)(3) (3) Whenever appropriate after an unanticipated food safety problem in accordance with § 117.150(b); and
(b)(4) (4) Whenever you find that a preventive control, combination of preventive controls, or the food safety plan as a whole is ineffective.
(c) (c) You must complete the reanalysis required by paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section and validate, as appropriate to the nature of the preventive control and its role in the facility's food safety system, any additional preventive controls needed to address the hazard identified:
(c)(1) (1) Before any change in activities (including any change in preventive control) at the facility is operative; or
(c)(2) (2) When necessary to demonstrate the control measures can be implemented as designed:
(c)(2)(i) (i) Within 90 calendar days after production of the applicable food first begins; or
(c)(2)(ii) (ii) Within a reasonable timeframe, provided that the preventive controls qualified individual prepares (or oversees the preparation of) a written justification for a timeframe that exceeds 90-calendar days after production of the applicable food first begins.
(d) (d) You must revise the written food safety plan if a significant change in the activities conducted at your facility creates a reasonable potential for a new hazard or a significant increase in a previously identified hazard or document the basis for the conclusion that no revisions are needed.
(e) (e) A preventive controls qualified individual must perform (or oversee) the reanalysis.
(f) (f) You must conduct a reanalysis of the food safety plan when FDA determines it is necessary to respond to new hazards and developments in scientific understanding.
